stem: What is the approximate acceleration of free fall near the Earth's surface?

options.rationale: Ten times too small.
Correct.
Ten times too big.
Wrong unit: that is a speed.

explanation: g is about 9.8 m/s² near the Earth's surface.

stem: A hammer and a feather are dropped together inside a tube from which all the air has been removed. What happens?

options.rationale: In a vacuum there is no air resistance to slow the feather.
Nothing pushes the feather down faster.
Correct: both accelerate at g.
Without air the feather falls like everything else.

explanation: With no air resistance every object falls with the same acceleration g, whatever its mass.

stem: A coin is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving after $3.0\ \text{s}$? Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
An object falls from rest without air resistance. How long does it take to reach a speed of $49\ \text{m/s}$? Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
hints: The speed increases by 9.8 m/s every second.

stem: When a falling object reaches terminal velocity, the resultant force on it is zero.
explanation: At terminal velocity the air resistance equals the weight, so the forces balance and the speed stays constant.

stem: Why does the acceleration of a skydiver decrease as she falls before opening her parachute?

options.content: Her weight decreases as she falls.
options.rationale: Her weight stays the same.

options.content: Air resistance increases with speed, so the resultant force decreases.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Gravity is weaker closer to the ground.
options.rationale: The change over a few kilometres is tiny.
Mass does not change.

explanation: As her speed rises, air resistance rises, so weight − air resistance (the resultant force) gets smaller, and so does her acceleration.
hints: Think about how the resultant force changes.

stem: A skydiver at terminal velocity opens her parachute. What happens immediately afterwards?

options.rationale: She still moves down; she slows down.
The extra air resistance acts upwards.

options.content: She slows down because air resistance is now greater than her weight.
options.rationale: Correct.
The forces are no longer balanced.

explanation: The large parachute suddenly increases air resistance above her weight; the resultant force is upwards, so she decelerates until a new, lower terminal velocity is reached.
hints: Compare the air resistance with the weight just after the parachute opens.

stem: A skydiver of mass $80\ \text{kg}$ falls at a constant (terminal) velocity before opening her parachute. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{N/kg}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the air resistance on her at terminal velocity?
parts.explanation: At terminal velocity air resistance $=$ weight $= mg = 80 \times 9.8 = 784\ \text{N}$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. At terminal velocity air resistance $=$ weight $= mg = 80 \times 9.8 = 784\ \text{N}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why her speed is constant.

points.description: The air resistance (upwards) equals her weight (downwards), so the resultant force is zero
With no resultant force there is no acceleration, so the velocity stays constant

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Just after the parachute opens, which way does the resultant force on her act?

options.rationale: Correct: air resistance is now larger than the weight.
The weight is now smaller than the air resistance.
The forces are unbalanced just after opening.
Both forces are vertical.

parts.explanation: Air resistance exceeds weight, so the resultant force is upwards and she decelerates.

explanation: Terminal velocity: air resistance = weight = 784 N, resultant force zero. Opening the parachute makes air resistance larger than the weight: resultant force upwards, so she slows.
hints: At terminal velocity the forces are balanced.

stem: Match each stage of a skydive with the correct description of the forces.

right.content: Air resistance very small; acceleration about 9.8 m/s²

explanation: The resultant force (weight − air resistance) controls the acceleration at each stage.
hints: Air resistance grows as speed grows.

stem: To measure $g$, a learner drops a steel ball from rest through a height of $1.25\ \text{m}$. An electronic timer records a fall time of $0.505\ \text{s}$. Use $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ to calculate $g$.
What name is given to the constant maximum velocity of an object falling through air, when air resistance balances its weight?
A flat sheet of paper and an identical sheet crumpled into a tight ball are dropped together in air. What happens?

options.content: The flat sheet lands first because it is wider.
options.rationale: Its larger area gives more air resistance, so it falls more slowly.

options.content: They land together because they have the same mass.
options.rationale: This would be true only in a vacuum.

options.content: The crumpled ball lands first because it is heavier.
options.rationale: Both have the same mass.

options.content: The crumpled ball lands first because it has less air resistance.
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: Same mass and weight, but the flat sheet meets much more air resistance, so it has a much smaller terminal velocity.

stem: Without air resistance, a heavy stone falls with a greater acceleration than a light stone.
explanation: Without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration, g.

stem: Which describes the speed-time graph of a skydiver from jumping until she reaches terminal velocity (parachute still closed)?

options.rationale: That would be constant acceleration all the way.
She starts from rest.

options.content: A curve that gets steeper and steeper
options.rationale: Her acceleration decreases, not increases.

options.content: A curve that starts steep and levels off to a horizontal line
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: The gradient (acceleration) starts at about 9.8 m/s² and decreases to zero as air resistance grows, so the curve levels off at terminal velocity.
hints: The gradient of a speed-time graph is the acceleration.

stem: A ball is dropped from rest. Its speed-time graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$. Using the area under the graph, how far does it fall in the first $2.0\ \text{s}$?
explanation: After $2.0\ \text{s}$ the speed is $19.6\ \text{m/s}$; the area of the triangle $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 19.6 = 19.6\ \text{m}$.
workedSolution: 1. After $2.0\ \text{s}$ the speed is $19.6\ \text{m/s}$; the area of the triangle $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 19.6 = 19.6\ \text{m}$.
hints: Find the speed at 2.0 s first.
